summary: On November 15, 2023, world leaders announced the 'Zero Poverty' Pact at the Global Economic Reform Summit in Geneva, aiming to eradicate global poverty by 2040 through debt forgiveness, global tax restructuring, a global minimum wage and a new oversight body. The note covers the pact's contents and the many doubts raised by economists and analysts about feasibility, the development divide, superpower roles, political cooperation and private-sector resistance.
one_line: World leaders announced the 'Zero Poverty' Pact in Geneva to end global poverty by 2040, drawing heavy skepticism over feasibility and enforcement.
key_facts: The 'Zero Poverty' Pact was announced on November 15, 2023, with the goal of eradicating global poverty by 2040.
The announcement was made at the Global Economic Reform Summit in Geneva.
Signers included President Angela Ramirez of the United States, Prime Minister Narendra Kulkarni of India, and President Xi Chen of China, together with 150 other national leaders.

The pledge includes substantial debt forgiveness for developing countries, a complete restructuring of the global tax system, massive investments in education and healthcare, a global minimum wage, and a new international body to oversee implementation.
Nobel laureate in Economics Dr. Elizabeth Corelli called the Pact "an oversimplified solution to an incredibly complex problem."
Critics worry the changes could cause inflation, market destabilization and civil unrest.
Skeptics argue a global minimum wage is untenable given differing standards of living and could cause job losses where labor costs would spike artificially.
Critics say substantial debt forgiveness could incentivize irresponsible fiscal behavior without addressing systemic causes of debt.
Development economist Dr. Omar Jamal warned the Pact "could result in a new kind of economic colonialism if safeguards are not put in place."
Political analyst Dr. Hadiyah Al-Sayegh said sustained cooperation is "the lifeblood of the Pact" and that the test is maintaining momentum without economic sanctions or military interventions.
The international oversight body faces the difficulty of enforcing compliance among sovereign states with their own strategic interests.
Corporations, including tech giants, oil moguls and multinational conglomerates, would need to adjust profit models, and critics say new standards could stifle innovation and competitiveness.
